solution: \(\sin^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(\sin\) restricted to its principal branch \(\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), on which \(\sin\) is a bijection onto \([-1, 1]\). So \(y = \sin^{-1}x\) always lies in that CLOSED interval, and both endpoints are attained: \(x = -1\) gives \(y = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = 1\) gives \(y = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\) — which is why the OPEN interval \(\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is not the answer. The ranges \([0, \pi]\) and \((0, \pi)\) describe the \(\cos^{-1}\) branch, not this one. Hence \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2} \le y \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\), since \(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\) lies in the principal range \(\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\). For \(\sec^{-1}(-2)\) the principal range is \([0, \pi]\) with \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) removed, and \(\sec\theta = -2\) means \(\cos\theta = -\tfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\theta = \tfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Hence the value is \(\tfrac{\pi}{3} - \tfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\tfrac{\pi}{3}\), confirmed numerically: \(\arctan\sqrt{3} - \arccos(-0.5) = -1.0471975512\).

\(\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\) lies outside the principal range \([0, \pi]\) of \(\cos^{-1}\), so it cannot be the value however tempting it looks. Now \(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6} = -\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), and the unique \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) with \(\cos\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) is \(\theta = \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\). Verified numerically: \(\arccos\left(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) = 2.6179938780 = \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\).

\(\sin^{-1}\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), taking the principal branch \(\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\). The argument is therefore \(\tfrac{\pi}{3} - \left(-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \tfrac{\pi}{3} + \tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\), and \(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\). Verified numerically: \(\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3} - \arcsin(-0.5)\right) = 1.0\) exactly.

\(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\). The principal range of \(\cot^{-1}\) is \((0, \pi)\), so \(\cot^{-1}\left(-\sqrt{3}\right)\) is the \(\theta \in (0, \pi)\) with \(\cot\theta = -\sqrt{3}\), namely \(\theta = \pi - \tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\) — NOT \(-\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), which lies outside the branch. Hence \(\tfrac{\pi}{3} - \tfrac{5\pi}{6} = \tfrac{2\pi}{6} - \tfrac{5\pi}{6} = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\). Verified numerically: \(\cot^{-1}\left(-\sqrt{3}\right) = 2.6179938780 = \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and the difference is \(-1.5707963268 = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).

Put \(\theta = \tan^{-1}x\), so \(\tan\theta = x\) with \(\theta \in \left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), where \(\cos\theta > 0\). Then \(\sec^{2}\theta = 1 + x^{2}\) gives \(\cos\theta = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\), so \(\sin\theta = \tan\theta\,\cos\theta = \tfrac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\). The forms carrying \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) belong to \(\sin\left(\cos^{-1}x\right)\)-type identities, not this one. Verified numerically at \(x = -0.9,\ -0.3,\ 0,\ 0.4,\ 0.87\): \(\sin\left(\arctan x\right)\) matches \(\tfrac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\) to machine precision in every case.

Domain: \(\sin^{-1}(1-x)\) needs \(x \in [0, 2]\) and \(\sin^{-1}x\) needs \(x \in [-1, 1]\), so \(x\) lies in \([0, 1]\). Rewrite as \(\sin^{-1}(1-x) = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\sin^{-1}x\) and take sine: \(1 - x = \sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\sin^{-1}x\right) = \cos\left(2\sin^{-1}x\right) = 1 - 2x^{2}\), so \(2x^{2} - x = 0\) and the CANDIDATES are \(x = 0\) and \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}\). Compounding can introduce extraneous roots, so both were tested in the ORIGINAL equation: at \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\sin^{-1}\tfrac{1}{2} - 2\sin^{-1}\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{6} - \tfrac{\pi}{3} = -\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), not \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) (residual \(-2.0944\)), so \(x = \tfrac{1}{2}\) is extraneous; at \(x = 0\), \(\sin^{-1}(1) - 0 = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\) exactly (residual \(0.0\)). A 2001-point scan of the residual over the whole domain \([0, 1]\) found no other sign change, so \(x = 0\) is the only solution — the un-filtered candidate pairs \(\left\{0,\ \tfrac{1}{2}\right\}\) and \(\left\{1,\ \tfrac{1}{2}\right\}\) are the traps for skipping the extraneous-root check.
